text: (I’m a big fan of geographic and family-based community. Ideological communities, like those formed by people who want similar careers or who want to build similar products, are great but insufficient. Ideological communities alone are echo chambers.)

text: For communities, remote work helps people visit and return to places they’re already invested in, or maybe even never move in the first place. And that means more time spent with different kinds of people.

author: embirico
text: For individuals, remote work enables more choice and living on your own terms.

author: embirico
text:
Enter remote work: Flexibility to unbundle key career decisions from personal decisions.
Like where to live, or whether you can take time to care for family.

author: embirico
text: Even if you’re building a pure software product—especially if you’re building a pure software product, you should be spending time with people outside of tech.

author: embirico
text: And that’s how the most influential products are made by people who mostly hang out with similar people, who mostly work in the same industry. Not a good situation.

author: embirico
text:
If you’re interested in tech today, there’s an incredibly strong pull to SF, NY (& Miami?). A lot of people like me move to invest in our careers.
One of the easiest ways to make friends when you’re new and young? Colleagues at work, and their friends.

author: embirico
text:
Unpacking some of these:

- Smaller video -> people feel further away -> not in your personal space

- Looking at faces is emotionally stimulating. Do it when you want that stimulation and skip it otherwise.

- Looking at yourself is a self-evaluatory behavior. Exhausting.

author: embirico
text:
Zoom fatigue doesn't have to be. You can:
- Write or record work
- Make video smaller or turn it off
- Focus on content not faces
- Hide your own video
- Walk around
- Shift why you talk from executing to bonding & ideating
- Unschedule your mtgs -> talk when you feel like it
